Imagine someone at a formal dinner who loudly burps, makes a crude sexual joke, and uses offensive language — and does it all with zero awareness that it bothers everyone around them. The quality of their behavior, the crudeness and offensiveness of it, is what we call vulgarity.

In its simplest form, vulgarity is the quality of being crude, offensive, or lacking in taste and refinement — in a way that embarrasses, offends, or disgusts others.

The word "vulgarity" works in two distinct ways:

1. As an abstract quality (uncountable)

Here, "vulgarity" refers to the general state or nature of something being crude or offensive. You cannot put "a" before it, and you cannot make it plural in this sense.

  • "The vulgarity of his jokes made everyone uncomfortable."
  • "She was shocked by the vulgarity of the scene in the film."
  • "There is a certain vulgarity to that kind of humor."

Think of it like the word "heat" — you don't say "a heat" or "heats" when talking about the general quality. Similarly, in this sense, vulgarity is the invisible quality that makes something crude.

2. As a specific crude act or word (countable)

Here, "a vulgarity" or "vulgarities" refers to a specific crude word, phrase, gesture, or act — a particular instance of being vulgar.

  • "He muttered a vulgarity under his breath."
  • "Her speech was filled with vulgarities that shocked the audience."
  • "The comedian relied too heavily on vulgarities for laughs."

In this sense, a "vulgarity" is almost like a unit of crudeness — one specific rude word, one offensive gesture, one tasteless remark.

Vulgarity is not limited to just one type of behavior. It covers a wide range:

Language: Using crude, indecent, or obscene words. Swear words and sexually explicit language are the most common examples. Saying something offensive about a person's body, for instance, is a vulgarity.

Humor: Jokes that rely on bodily functions, crude sexual references, or offensive stereotypes are considered vulgar. The humor is not clever or witty — it is simply crude and shock-based.

Behavior and manners: Actions that are grossly rude or indecent in a social setting — like spitting, making obscene gestures, or behaving in an sexually inappropriate way in public.

Content in art, media, or writing: A film, book, or painting can be described as having vulgarity if it features crude, gratuitous, or tasteless content purely for shock value, with no meaningful purpose.

Vulgarity exists on a spectrum. Not all vulgarity is equal.

At the mild end, a slightly rude joke among friends might be called a "minor vulgarity." At the extreme end, deeply offensive and obscene language or behavior would be called gross vulgarity. The word can describe anything along this range, and context determines where something falls.

This is an important nuance: what counts as vulgarity depends on context, culture, and audience.

A crude joke between close friends in private may not feel vulgar. The same joke told at a child's birthday party or a professional meeting would absolutely be considered vulgar. The setting and audience matter enormously.

Similarly, across different cultures and historical periods, the line between "acceptable" and "vulgar" has shifted. What one society considers normal, another may find deeply offensive.

This means vulgarity is partly objective (some things are widely recognized as crude across most cultures) and partly subjective (some things depend on who is watching and where).

A key part of understanding "vulgarity" is understanding the reaction it produces in others. Vulgarity typically makes people feel:

  • Offended — it crosses a line of decency
  • Embarrassed — especially if they are present when it happens
  • Disgusted — it feels beneath acceptable standards of behavior
  • Uncomfortable — it violates the unspoken rules of polite society

This reaction is what separates vulgarity from something that is merely unconventional or controversial. Vulgarity is not just unusual — it is actively crude or distasteful.

To sharpen your understanding, here is what "vulgarity" does not mean:

  • It does not mean simply being rude or unkind. Saying something cruel or hurtful is not automatically vulgar. Vulgarity specifically involves crudeness and indecency, not just general meanness.
  • It does not mean being incorrect or wrong. A factual mistake is not a vulgarity.
  • It does not mean being informal or casual. Speaking casually or using slang is not the same as being vulgar. Vulgarity carries a sense of indecency and poor taste, not just informality.
  • It is not the same as obscenity, though the two overlap. Obscenity is a stronger, often legal term for deeply offensive content. Vulgarity is the broader, everyday term for crudeness and bad taste in general.

• Vulgar (adjective) — the describing word: "That was a vulgar comment."
  • Vulgarly (adverb) — describing how something is done: "He spoke vulgarly."
  • Vulgarities (plural noun) — multiple crude words or acts: "The show was full of vulgarities."
  • Vulgarize (verb) — to make something vulgar or crude: "He vulgarized an otherwise elegant story."

Vulgarity is the quality of being crude, indecent, or offensively lacking in taste — whether in words, humor, behavior, or content — and it is something that tends to offend, embarrass, or disgust the people who witness it.
